It is related that al-Rayyan ibn Halmalah said: The chiefs of Quraysh and Abu Jahl said: "The matter of Muhammad has become confused for us. So let us seek a man knowledgeable in poetry, soothsaying and magic, let him speak with him and then come to us with a clear account of his affair." Utbah ibn Rabi'ah said: "By Allah, I have heard soothsaying, poetry and magic, and I know of these a knowledge that is not hidden from me, if that is what it is." They said: "Go to him and speak with him." So he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "O Muhammad, are you better, or Qusayy ibn Kilab? Are you better, or Hashim? Are you better, or Abd al-Muttalib? Are you better, or Abdullah? Then why do you revile our gods, mislead our forefathers, belittle our minds, and disparage our religion? If you seek leadership, we will make you our leader for as long as you live; if you seek marriage, we will marry you to ten women from whichever daughters of Quraysh you choose; if you seek wealth, we will gather for you enough wealth to make you and your descendants rich after you; and if what comes to you is a spirit (ri'y) from the jinn that has overcome you, we will spend our wealth seeking a cure for you, or we will be defeated on your account." The Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent. When he finished, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Have you finished, Abu al-Walid?" He said: "Yes."

(He said: "Then listen to me") [[The addition is from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]] He said: "O nephew, I am listening." He (ﷺ) said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Mim. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A Book whose verses have been detailed, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who have knowledge," up to the words: ﴿If they turn away, then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13]. Then Utbah leapt up, placed his hand over the mouth of the Prophet (ﷺ), and adjured him by Allah and by the ties of kinship to be silent. He returned to his family and did not go out to the Quraysh. Abu Jahl came to him and said: "Have you inclined toward Muhammad? Or has his food pleased you?" Utbah became angry and swore that he would never speak to Muhammad again. Then he said: "By Allah, you know that I am among the wealthiest of Quraysh, but when I related the account to him, he answered me with something that, by Allah, is neither poetry nor soothsaying nor magic." Then he recited to them what he had heard from him up to His words: ﴿like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13], and said: "I put my hand over his mouth and adjured him by the ties of kinship to desist. You know that when Muhammad says something, he does not lie. By Allah, I feared that punishment would descend upon you," meaning the thunderbolt. Abu Bakr al-Anbari related this report in his book al-Radd from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited "Ha, Mim. Fussilat" until he reached the prostration and prostrated, while Utbah was listening attentively, leaning on his hands behind his back. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished the recitation, he said to him: "O Abu al-Walid, you have heard what I recited to you, so the matter is up to you." Utbah returned to the Quraysh in their assembly. They said: "By Allah, Abu al-Walid has come back to you with a face other than the one with which he left you." Then they said: "What is your news, Abu al-Walid?" He said: "By Allah, I have heard words from Muhammad such as I have never heard before. By Allah, it is neither poetry nor soothsaying. So obey me in this and leave the matter to me: leave Muhammad to himself and withdraw from him. By Allah, what I have heard from his words will certainly have a consequence. If the Arabs overcome him, you will be relieved of him by the hands of others; and if he is a king or a prophet, you will be the happiest of people in him, for his kingdom is your kingdom and his honour is your honour." They said: "Far-fetched! Muhammad has bewitched you, Abu al-Walid." He said: "This is my opinion for you; do as you wish."

Al-Farra' and others said this is its meaning. It was said: it is a screen preventing response. It was also said: Abu Jahl covered his head with a garment and said: "O Muhammad, between us and you is a barrier," as mockery. This is related by al-Naqqash and mentioned by al-Qushayri. So "hijab" here is the garment. "So act, for we are acting," meaning: act for our destruction, for we are acting for your destruction, as said by al-Kalbi. Muqatil said: act for your god who sent you, for we act for our gods whom we worship. It was also said: act according to what your religion requires, for we act according to what our religion requires. It may also bear a fifth meaning [[The author mentioned only four views; perhaps the fifth is what al-Kashshaf mentions: "So act in the abolishing of our affair, for we are acting in the abolishing of yours."]]: act for your afterlife, for we act for our worldly life, as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 41, verses 6–8:**

God's words: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you.﴾ That is, I am not an angel; rather, I am from the children of Adam. Al-Hasan said: God taught him humility.

"It is revealed to me" means from the heavens, through the hands of the angels, "that your God is one God." "So" believe in Him, "and go straight toward Him," that is, turn your faces toward Him in supplication and in asking of Him, as a man says, "Go straight to your home," meaning do not turn aside to anything other than the intention to reach your home. "And ask His forgiveness" means for your shirk (associating partners with God).

"And woe to the polytheists who do not give zakat" (obligatory almsgiving). Ibn Abbas said: they do not bear witness that "there is no god but God," and this is the zakat of the souls. Qatada said: they do not acknowledge that zakat is obligatory. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: they do not give charity and do not spend in obedience. He rebuked them for stinginess, which noble people find shameful. This indicates that the disbeliever is punished for his disbelief together with the prevention of zakat being obligatory upon him. Al-Farra' and others said: the polytheists used to spend money, give drink to the pilgrims and feed them, but they forbade this to whoever believed in Muhammad ﷺ, so this verse was revealed about them. "And they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers." Therefore they do not spend in obedience, do not go straight, and do not seek forgiveness.

Al-Zamakhshari: If you ask, why was the withholding of zakat singled out among the attributes of the polytheists, and linked with disbelief in the Hereafter? I say: because the thing most beloved to a person is his wealth, and it is the twin of his spirit. When he gives it up in the way of God, that is the strongest proof of his steadfastness, his uprightness, the sincerity of his intention, and the purity of his inner disposition. Do you not see His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and for the strengthening of their souls﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265], meaning they strengthen their souls, and they demonstrate their firmness by spending wealth. The hearts that were won over were only enticed by a trifle (lumdhah) of worldly goods. The lumdhah in the language is a speck of whiteness or blackness, and what is meant here is a small amount of worldly wreckage. Thus their band grew strong and their resolve softened. The apostates after the Messenger of God ﷺ only rose up by withholding zakat, so wars were waged against them and they were fought. In this there is an incitement to the believers to pay zakat and a severe warning against withholding it, since withholding has been made one of the attributes of the polytheists and linked with disbelief in the Hereafter.

God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "ghayr mamnun" means uncut, derived from manantu al-habl, when I cut the rope. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Isba':

By your life, my door is not one that is bolted
against the friend, nor is my goodness cut off.
[Another narration: "nor is my provision cut off."]

And another said:

Then you see behind her, from the dust and the gusts,
weak dust-clouds, as if they were scattered motes.

By al-mannin he means the weak, cut-off dust. Also from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil: "ghayr mamnun" means not diminished. From this comes al-manun, because it diminishes a person, that is, his strength. Qutrub said, and he recited the verse of Zuhayr:

The excellence of the swift over the slow horses, so it
does not give, through that, anything cut off or hasty.
[The verse is from a qasida in praise of Harim ibn Sinan.]

Al-Jawhari said: al-mann is cutting, and it is said to mean diminishing, and from it is God's words: ﴿They have a reward that is not diminished.﴾ And Labid said:

...the swift, keen-eyed, whose food is not reduced
[The first half of the verse:
"A carcass-stripping, fierce pack contending over its remains."
This verse occurred as an error in some copies of al-Jawhari, so check its verification in Lisan al-Arab under the root "mann."]

Mujahid said: "ghayr mamnun" means not counted. It was also said: "ghayr mamnun" means not bestowed upon them as a favor. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the chronically ill, the sick, and the aged, who when they become too weak for obedience, there is recorded for them a reward like the best of what they used to do when they were able.

The hearts that were won over were only enticed by a trifle (lumdhah) of worldly goods. The lumdhah in the language is a speck of whiteness or blackness, and what is meant here is a small amount of worldly wreckage. Thus their band grew strong and their resolve softened. The apostates after the Messenger of God ﷺ only rose up by withholding zakat, so wars were waged against them and they were fought. In this there is an incitement to the believers to pay zakat and a severe warning against withholding it, since withholding has been made one of the attributes of the polytheists and linked with disbelief in the Hereafter.

God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "ghayr mamnun" means uncut, derived from manantu al-habl, when I cut the rope. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Isba':

By your life, my door is not one that is bolted
against the friend, nor is my goodness cut off.
[Another narration: "nor is my provision cut off."]

And another said:

Then you see behind her, from the dust and the gusts,
weak dust-clouds, as if they were scattered motes.

By al-mannin he means the weak, cut-off dust. Also from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil: "ghayr mamnun" means not diminished. From this comes al-manun, because it diminishes a person, that is, his strength. Qutrub said, and he recited the verse of Zuhayr:

The excellence of the swift over the slow horses, so it
does not give, through that, anything cut off or hasty.
[The verse is from a qasida in praise of Harim ibn Sinan.]

Al-Jawhari said: al-mann is cutting, and it is said to mean diminishing, and from it is God's words: ﴿They have a reward that is not diminished.﴾ And Labid said:

...the swift, keen-eyed, whose food is not reduced
[The first half of the verse:
"A carcass-stripping, fierce pack contending over its remains."
This verse occurred as an error in some copies of al-Jawhari, so check its verification in Lisan al-Arab under the root "mann."]

Mujahid said: "ghayr mamnun" means not counted. It was also said: "ghayr mamnun" means not bestowed upon them as a favor. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the chronically ill, the sick, and the aged, who when they become too weak for obedience, there is recorded for them a reward like the best of what they used to do when they were able.

**Verse 9–12 of Surah Fussilat (41)**

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days?﴾ The reading of *a-innakum* is with two hamzas, the second being between-between (*bayna bayn*), and also *a-innakum* with an alif between two hamzas. It is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke. He was commanded to rebuke them and to express wonder at their action, meaning: why do you disbelieve in Allah, when He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth? ﴿In two days﴾, namely Sunday and Monday. ﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾, meaning equals and partners. ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds.﴾

﴿And He placed in it﴾, meaning in the earth, ﴿firm mountains from above it﴾, meaning the mountains. Wahb said: When Allah created the earth, it shook over the surface of the water, so He said to Jibril: "Steady it, O Jibril." He descended and held it, but the winds overpowered him. He said: "O Lord, You know best; I have been overpowered by it." So He steadied it with the mountains and fixed it firmly. ﴿And He blessed it﴾ by what He created in it of benefits. As-Suddi said: He caused its trees to grow. ﴿And apportioned in it its sustenance﴾. As-Suddi and al-Hasan said: the provisions of its inhabitants and their welfare. Qatadah and Mujahid said: He created in it its rivers, its trees and its animals, on Tuesday and Wednesday. Ikrimah and ad-Dahhak said: the meaning of ﴿apportioned in it its sustenance﴾ is the provisions of its inhabitants and what suits their livelihoods, of trades, trees and benefits, in every land, what He did not place in another, so that some of them may live by means of others through trade and travel from one land to another. Ikrimah said: To the extent that in some lands they exchange gold for salt, weight for equal weight. Mujahid and ad-Dahhak said: the *sabiri* (a type of cloth) from Sabur, the *tayalisah* (shawls) from ar-Rayy, and the Yemeni *hubur* (striped garments) from Yemen.

﴿In four days﴾, meaning in the completion of four days. An example of this is the saying of a speaker: "I went out from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and to Kufa in fifteen days", meaning in the completion of fifteen days. Ibn al-Anbari and others said this.

﴿Equally for those who ask﴾. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "in four days, equal and complete." Al-Farra' said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "And He apportioned in it its sustenance, equally for those in need." Al-Tabari chose this view. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Ya'qub al-Hadrami read *sawa'in lil-sa'ilin* with the genitive (*jarr*). Ibn al-Qa'qa' read *sawa'un* with the nominative (*raf'*). The accusative (*nasb*) is as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and *sawa'an* means *istiwa'* (equality), i.e., they became equal in equality. It is also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance (*hal*) and of separation (*qat'*). The genitive is as an attribute (*na't*) of *ayyam* or of *arba'a*, meaning "in four days" that are equal and complete. The nominative is as the subject (*mubtada'*) with the predicate *lil-sa'ilin*, or by implying "this is equal for those who ask." The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: the meaning of ﴿equally for those who ask﴾ and for those who do not ask, i.e., He created the earth and what is in it for whoever asks and whoever does not ask, and He gives to whoever asks and whoever does not ask.

Allah's statement: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾, meaning He resolved to create it and intended to shape it. Istiwa' (turning to, rising) is, according to most opinions, one of the attributes of actions. This is shown by Allah's statement: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and the discussion of that has already passed there [See vol. 1, p. 254 and following, second or third printing]. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ that it means: His command ascended to the heaven. Al-Hasan also said so. Whoever says it is an essential attribute added to His essence says: He turned to it in eternity with His attributes. The *thumma* ("then") refers to the transition of the heaven from the state of smoke to the state of density. That smoke was from the breath of the water when it breathed, as has passed in al-Baqarah from Ibn Mas'ud and others.

﴿And He said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾, meaning: bring forth what I have placed in you of benefits and interests and bring them out for My creation. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah said to the heaven: "Make your sun, your moon and your stars rise, and send forth your winds and your clouds." And He said to the earth: "Split open your rivers and bring out your trees and your fruits, obediently or unwillingly." ﴿They said: We come willingly.﴾ In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: "We come to Your command willingly." It is also said: the meaning of this command is subjugation, i.e., "Be!" and they were, as He said: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. On this view He said that before creating them. On the first view He said it after creating them, and this is the view of the majority. In His statement to them there are two possibilities. The first is that it was a speech that He spoke. The second is that it was a power from Him that became manifest to them, which took the place of speech in attaining the purpose; al-Mawardi mentioned this. ﴿They said: We come willingly.﴾ There are also two possibilities here. The first is that the manifestation of obedience from them, in that they submitted and responded, took the place of their saying, and from this is the saying of the rajiz (poet):

The pool filled and said: "Enough, gently, I have filled my belly."

meaning that this appeared in it. Most of the people of knowledge said: Rather, Allah created speech in them both, and they spoke as He willed. Abu Nasr as-Sukasiki said: The place of the Ka'bah spoke from the earth, and what was opposite it spoke from the heaven, and Allah placed His sanctuary in it. He said *ta'i'in* ("willing") and did not say *ta'i'atayn* ("two willing females") in keeping with the form, nor *ta'i'at* ("willing females") in keeping with the meaning, because they are heavens and earths. He reported about them and about those in them. It is also said: when He described them with speech and response, which are attributes of rational beings, He treated them in the pronoun as rational beings, as in the similar verse: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4], and this has already been discussed [See vol. 7, p. 344, and vol. 9, p. 122, first or second printing].

In a hadith: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, if the heavens and the earth, when You said to them, 'Come willingly or unwillingly,' had disobeyed You, what would You have done with them?" He said: "I would have commanded one of My creatures, and it would have swallowed them." He said: "O Lord, where is that creature?" He said: "In a meadow of My meadows." He said: "O Lord, where is that meadow?" He said: "A knowledge of My knowledge." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah read *a-tayya* with the long vowel and fatha (*ata-yā*). Likewise His statement: *ata-yna ta'i'in*, meaning: "Give obedience from yourselves." *Qalatā* ("they said"): "We gave, obediently," with both objects omitted together. It is also possible, and it is better, that *atayna* be *a'lamna* (a form of the verb meaning "we came"), in which case one object is omitted. Whoever reads *atayna* ("we came"), the meaning is "we came with what is in us," as has been explained previously in more than one place, praise be to Allah.

Allah's statement: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾, meaning He perfected them and finished them. It is also said: He made them firm, as the poet said [the poet is Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali; *al-sani'* means the skilled one]:

And upon them two coats of mail, which Dawud completed, or which Tubba' the skilled made as wide, complete coats.

"In two days", apart from the four days in which He created the earth, so the creation of the heavens and the earth occurred in six days, as Allah said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], as has been explained earlier in al-A'raf [See vol. 7, p. 219, first or second printing]. Mujahid said: And one day of the six days is like a thousand years of what you count. From 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: Allah created the earth in two days, and apportioned in it its sustenance in two days, and created the heavens in two days. He created the earth on Sunday and Monday, apportioned in it its sustenance on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens on Thursday and Friday. The last hour of Friday is when Allah created Adam, in haste, and it is the hour in which the Hour will be established, and there is no creature created by Allah except that it is frightened on Friday, except humans and jinn. This is the view of the commentators, except for what Muslim related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my two hands and said: "Allah created the clay on Saturday..." the hadith. We have discussed its chain of narration at the beginning of Surah al-An'am [See vol. 6, p. 384, first or second printing].

﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾. Qatadah and as-Suddi said: He created in it its sun, its moon, its stars and its orbits, and He created in each heaven its creatures of angels and the creation that is in it, of seas, mountains of hail and snow. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: And for Allah, in each heaven there is a house, which the angels circumambulate, opposite the Ka'bah, and the one in the lowest heaven is the Bayt al-Ma'mur. It is also said: Allah revealed in each heaven, i.e., He revealed in it what He willed and what He commanded in it. Revelation (*wahy*) may also be a command, as in His statement: ﴿Because your Lord revealed to it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], and His statement: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 111], meaning I commanded them, and this is a command of creation.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning with shining stars. It is also said: in each heaven there are shining stars. It is also said: rather the stars are specific to the lowest heaven. ﴿And as protection﴾, meaning We protected it with protection, from the devils who eavesdrop. This protection is by the stars with which the devils are pelted, as has been explained earlier in al-Hijr [See vol. 10, p. 10, first or second printing].

The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the earth was created before the heaven. But in another verse He said: ﴿Is the heaven He built [more difficult to create]?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27], then said: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30], and this indicates that the heaven was created first. Some people said: the earth was created before the heaven. As for His statement ﴿and the earth after that He spread out﴾, the spreading out (*dahw*) is other than creation. So Allah created the earth, then created the heavens, then spread out the earth, i.e., extended it and spread it, said Ibn 'Abbas. This meaning has already been discussed thoroughly in al-Baqarah [See vol. 1, p. 255 and following, second or third printing], and praise be to Allah.

﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

The accusative (*nasb*) is as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and *sawa'an* means *istiwa'* (equality), i.e., they became equal in equality. It is also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance (*hal*) and of separation (*qat'*). The genitive is as an attribute (*na't*) of *ayyam* or of *arba'a*, meaning "in four days" that are equal and complete. The nominative is as the subject (*mubtada'*) with the predicate *lil-sa'ilin*, or by implying "this is equal for those who ask." The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: the meaning of ﴿equally for those who ask﴾ and for those who do not ask, i.e., He created the earth and what is in it for whoever asks and whoever does not ask, and He gives to whoever asks and whoever does not ask.

Allah's statement: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾, meaning He resolved to create it and intended to shape it. Istiwa' (turning to, rising) is, according to most opinions, one of the attributes of actions. This is shown by Allah's statement: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and the discussion of that has already passed there [See vol. 1, p. 254 and following, second or third printing]. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ that it means: His command ascended to the heaven. Al-Hasan also said so. Whoever says it is an essential attribute added to His essence says: He turned to it in eternity with His attributes. The *thumma* ("then") refers to the transition of the heaven from the state of smoke to the state of density. That smoke was from the breath of the water when it breathed, as has passed in al-Baqarah from Ibn Mas'ud and others.

﴿And He said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾, meaning: bring forth what I have placed in you of benefits and interests and bring them out for My creation. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah said to the heaven: "Make your sun, your moon and your stars rise, and send forth your winds and your clouds." And He said to the earth: "Split open your rivers and bring out your trees and your fruits, obediently or unwillingly." ﴿They said: We come willingly.﴾ In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: "We come to Your command willingly." It is also said: the meaning of this command is subjugation, i.e., "Be!" and they were, as He said: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. On this view He said that before creating them. On the first view He said it after creating them, and this is the view of the majority. In His statement to them there are two possibilities. The first is that it was a speech that He spoke. The second is that it was a power from Him that became manifest to them, which took the place of speech in attaining the purpose; al-Mawardi mentioned this. ﴿They said: We come willingly.﴾ There are also two possibilities here. The first is that the manifestation of obedience from them, in that they submitted and responded, took the place of their saying, and from this is the saying of the rajiz (poet):

The pool filled and said: "Enough, gently, I have filled my belly."

meaning that this appeared in it. Most of the people of knowledge said: Rather, Allah created speech in them both, and they spoke as He willed. Abu Nasr as-Sukasiki said: The place of the Ka'bah spoke from the earth, and what was opposite it spoke from the heaven, and Allah placed His sanctuary in it. He said *ta'i'in* ("willing") and did not say *ta'i'atayn* ("two willing females") in keeping with the form, nor *ta'i'at* ("willing females") in keeping with the meaning, because they are heavens and earths. He reported about them and about those in them. It is also said: when He described them with speech and response, which are attributes of rational beings, He treated them in the pronoun as rational beings, as in the similar verse: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4], and this has already been discussed [See vol. 7, p. 344, and vol. 9, p. 122, first or second printing].

In a hadith: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, if the heavens and the earth, when You said to them, 'Come willingly or unwillingly,' had disobeyed You, what would You have done with them?" He said: "I would have commanded one of My creatures, and it would have swallowed them." He said: "O Lord, where is that creature?" He said: "In a meadow of My meadows." He said: "O Lord, where is that meadow?" He said: "A knowledge of My knowledge." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah read *a-tayya* with the long vowel and fatha (*ata-yā*). Likewise His statement: *ata-yna ta'i'in*, meaning: "Give obedience from yourselves." *Qalatā* ("they said"): "We gave, obediently," with both objects omitted together. It is also possible, and it is better, that *atayna* be *a'lamna* (a form of the verb meaning "we came"), in which case one object is omitted. Whoever reads *atayna* ("we came"), the meaning is "we came with what is in us," as has been explained previously in more than one place, praise be to Allah.

Allah's statement: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾, meaning He perfected them and finished them. It is also said: He made them firm, as the poet said [the poet is Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali; *al-sani'* means the skilled one]:

And upon them two coats of mail, which Dawud completed, or which Tubba' the skilled made as wide, complete coats.

"In two days", apart from the four days in which He created the earth, so the creation of the heavens and the earth occurred in six days, as Allah said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], as has been explained earlier in al-A'raf [See vol. 7, p. 219, first or second printing]. Mujahid said: And one day of the six days is like a thousand years of what you count. From 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: Allah created the earth in two days, and apportioned in it its sustenance in two days, and created the heavens in two days. He created the earth on Sunday and Monday, apportioned in it its sustenance on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens on Thursday and Friday. The last hour of Friday is when Allah created Adam, in haste, and it is the hour in which the Hour will be established, and there is no creature created by Allah except that it is frightened on Friday, except humans and jinn. This is the view of the commentators, except for what Muslim related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my two hands and said: "Allah created the clay on Saturday..." the hadith. We have discussed its chain of narration at the beginning of Surah al-An'am [See vol. 6, p. 384, first or second printing].

﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾. Qatadah and as-Suddi said: He created in it its sun, its moon, its stars and its orbits, and He created in each heaven its creatures of angels and the creation that is in it, of seas, mountains of hail and snow. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: And for Allah, in each heaven there is a house, which the angels circumambulate, opposite the Ka'bah, and the one in the lowest heaven is the Bayt al-Ma'mur. It is also said: Allah revealed in each heaven, i.e., He revealed in it what He willed and what He commanded in it. Revelation (*wahy*) may also be a command, as in His statement: ﴿Because your Lord revealed to it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], and His statement: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 111], meaning I commanded them, and this is a command of creation.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning with shining stars. It is also said: in each heaven there are shining stars. It is also said: rather the stars are specific to the lowest heaven. ﴿And as protection﴾, meaning We protected it with protection, from the devils who eavesdrop. This protection is by the stars with which the devils are pelted, as has been explained earlier in al-Hijr [See vol. 10, p. 10, first or second printing].

﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

It is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke. He was commanded to rebuke them and to express wonder at their action, meaning: why do you disbelieve in Allah, when He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth? ﴿In two days﴾, namely Sunday and Monday. ﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾, meaning equals and partners. ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds.﴾

﴿And He placed in it﴾, meaning in the earth, ﴿firm mountains from above it﴾, meaning the mountains. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 13–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh, from what you, O Muhammad, call them to of faith. "Then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿAd and Thamud." That is, I have warned you of a destruction like the destruction of ʿAd and Thamud. "When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them," meaning those who were sent to them and to those before them. "Saying: Do not worship except Allah," the position of "an" (that) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e., "that you not worship" (ʾalla taʿbudu). "They said: If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels" instead of the messengers, "so indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent," of warning and good tidings. It has been said: this is mockery from them. It has also been said: they acknowledged that the messengers were sent, and after that came denial and obstinacy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for ʿAd, they were arrogant in the land﴾ over the servants of Allah, Hud and those who believed with him, "without right, and said: Who is mightier than us in strength?" They were deluded by their bodies when he threatened them with punishment, and they said: We are able to repel the punishment from ourselves by the excess of our strength. That was because they were people of tall bodies and great stature. It has already passed in [al-Aʿraf [see vol. 7, p. 236, first or second edition]] from Ibn ʿAbbas that the tallest of them was one hundred cubits and the shortest was sixty cubits. So Allah, exalted is He, answered them: "Do they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength" and power? A servant has power only by the empowerment of Allah, so Allah is then more capable. "And they were denying Our signs," that is, they were disbelieving in Our miracles.

His saying, exalted is He: "So We sent upon them a furious wind" (rihan sarsaran). This explains the thunderbolt which He sent upon them, that is, a wind that was cold, extremely cold, and violent in its sound and blowing. It is said: its origin is ṣarar, from ṣirr, which is cold [the addition is from al-Lisan, from Ibn al-Sikkit, because this speech is his]. Then the middle rāʾ was replaced by the first radical of the verb, as in their saying kabkabu, whose origin is kabbabu, and tajafjafa al-thawb, whose origin is tajaffafa. Abu ʿUbayda: the meaning of ṣarṣar is severe and stormy. ʿIkrima and Saʿid ibn Jubayr: extremely cold. Qutrub recited the verse of al-Hutayʾa:

"Those who feed when a ṣarṣara wind blows, and who bear (the burden) when they are asked for blood-money among the people."

Ustudu: when they are asked for the blood-money (diyya). Mujahid: extremely hot poisonous wind (samum). Maʿmar related from Qatada who said: cold. ʿAṭaʾ said the same, because "ṣarṣaran" is derived from ṣirr, and ṣirr in the speech of the Arabs means cold.

As someone said:

"For it is a shelter like the horns of women, set up on a day of wind and cold."

Al-Suddi said: intensely loud. From this comes ṣarra al-qalam wa al-bab, yaṣirru ṣarirran, meaning it made a sound. It is said: a dirham ṣarriyy and ṣirriyy for that which has a sound when it is struck. Ibn al-Sikkit said: ṣarṣar may be from ṣirr, which is cold, and it may be from the creaking of a door, and from ṣarra, which is a cry. From it is ﴿So his wife came forward in a cry﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 29]. Ṣarṣar is also the name of a river in Iraq.

"In days of ill omen" (nahisat), that is, unlucky, said by Mujahid and Qatada. They were from the last of Shawwal, from Wednesday to Wednesday, and that is ﴿seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Haqqa: 7]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: no people were punished except on a Wednesday. It is also said: "nahisat" means cold, related by al-Naqqash. It is also said: consecutive, from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAṭiyya. Al-Dahhak: severe. It is also said: full of dust, related by Ibn ʿIsa. From it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"He set out before the rising of the sun, for hunting, on a day of little ill omen."

Al-Dahhak and others said: Allah withheld rain from them for three years, and the winds blew upon them without rain. Some of them went out to Mecca to seek rain through it for the servants. In that time, when a trial or hardship befell people, they sought relief from Allah, exalted is He, and their seeking of that from Allah at His Sacred House, Mecca, was done by its Muslim and disbeliever alike. Thus many diverse people gathered in Mecca, of differing religions, and all of them revered Mecca, knowing its sanctity and its standing with Allah, exalted is He. Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah and al-Taymi said: when Allah wills good for a people, He sends rain upon them and withholds from them the abundance of winds; and when Allah wills evil for a people, He withholds rain from them and lets loose upon them the abundance of winds.

Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr recited "nahsat" with the ḥāʾ sukūn, as the plural of naḥs, which is a verbal noun used as an attribute. The rest recited "nahisat" with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, meaning possessors of ill omen. Among what indicates that naḥs is a verbal noun is His saying: ﴿on a day of continuous ill fortune﴾ [al-Qamar: 19]; had it been an attribute, the day would not have been made an annexed noun to it. On this Abu ʿAmr based his recitation, and Abu Hatim preferred it. Abu ʿUbayd preferred the second recitation and said: Abu ʿAmr's argument is not sound, because he made the day an annexed noun to naḥs with sukūn; it would have been a proof only if one made the day indefinite and described it, saying: ﴿on a day of naḥs﴾ [al-Qamar: 19], and no one we know has recited it so. Al-Mahdawi said: in "naḥs" only the sukūn has been heard. Al-Jawhari said: it is also read in His saying ﴿on a day of naḥs﴾ [al-Qamar: 19] as an attribute, but the annexation is more common and better. The word nahisa, with kasra, is also naḥis, as the poet said:

"Inform Judham and Lakhm that their brothers, Ṭayy and Bahraʾ, a people whose help is ill-omened."

From this it is said: days of ill omen (ayyam nahisat).

"That We may make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world," that is, so that We may make them taste the punishment by the sterile wind. "And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgraceful," that is, greater and more severe. "And they will not be helped."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾, meaning: We made clear to them the guidance (al-huda) and the misguidance (al-dalal), related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. Abu al-'Aliyah said: they chose blindness over clear proof. Al-Suddi said: they chose disobedience over obedience. ﴿So the punishment of humiliation seized them, the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment﴾. "Al-Hun" with a damma means humiliation (al-hawan). Hawn ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar, brother of Kinanah and Asad. And "ahanahu" means he belittled him; the noun is al-hawan and al-muhanah. The thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) is attributed to the punishment (al-'adhab) because "al-sa'iqah" is a name for that which annihilates and destroys, so it is as if he said: the destroying punishment, i.e., the punishment that destroys. And al-hawn, although it is a verbal noun (masdar), its meaning is humiliation (al-ihanah), and humiliation is a punishment, so it is permissible for one of the two to be made a description of the other, as if he said: the thunderbolt of humiliation. It is like your saying: "I have the knowledge of certainty" and "I have the certain knowledge." It may also be that al-hun is a noun like al-dun, and one says: "a humiliating punishment" (adhab hun), meaning humiliating (muhin), as He said: ﴿They remained in the punishment, the humiliating one﴾ [Saba': 14]. And it was said: meaning the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment. ﴿Because of what they used to earn﴾ from their denial of Salih and their hamstringing of the she-camel, as was mentioned earlier. ﴿And We saved those who believed﴾, meaning Salih and those who believed in him, i.e., We distinguished them from the disbelievers, so that what befell the disbelievers did not befall them. And thus, O Muhammad, do We deal with the believers of your people and their disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 19–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be driven in groups﴾. Nafi' read "nahshuru" with the nun, and "a'da'a" in the accusative. The rest read "yuhsharu" with a damma on the ya', and "a'da'u" in the nominative. The meaning of both is clear. The enemies of Allah are those who denied His messengers and opposed His command. "Fahum yuza'un" means they are driven and pushed toward Jahannam. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: the first of them is held back until the last of them joins them, so that they gather together. Abu al-Ahwas said: when the number is complete, they begin with the greatest in guilt, then the greatest.

The discussion of ﴿yuza'un﴾ [al-Naml: 17] has already been covered in full in "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 167 and following, first edition and its second.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: "Until, when they come to it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do." "Ma" here is superfluous (ziyadah). "Al-julud" (the skins) is taken, according to the view of most exegetes, to mean the skins themselves. Al-Suddi, Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far and al-Farra' said: by "al-julud" they meant the private parts (al-furuj). Some men of letters recited, citing 'Amir ibn Jawiyyah:

"The man strives for safety...
or the one whose skin is unharmed, whose head has turned white."

He said: "jiluduhu" is a metaphor for his private part. "And they say" — meaning the disbelievers — "to their skins: Why did you testify against us?" They were only arguing on your behalf. "They say: Allah has caused us to speak, He who causes everything to speak." Since they addressed and were addressed, they were treated as those who reason. "And He created you the first time" — that is, He placed life in you after you were drops of semen; whoever is able to do that is able to make the skins and the other limbs speak. It is also said: "And He created you the first time" is the beginning of a speech from Allah. "And to Him you will be returned."

In Sahih Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he laughed, and said: "Do you know what I am laughing at?" We said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "At the servant's address to his Lord, saying: O Lord, did You not protect me from injustice? He says: Yes. He says: Then I do not accept any witness against myself except one from myself. He says: Sufficient is your own self against you today as a witness, and the noble recording angels as witnesses. Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his limbs: Speak. So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left free to speak, and he says: Away with you, and destruction! It was for your sake that I was contending."

And in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Then it is said: Now we will send forth our witness against you." He reflects within himself: who is it that will testify against me? "But you supposed that Allah does not know much of what you do," of your deeds, so you disputed about that until your limbs testified against you about your deeds.

Bahz ibn Hakim narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding His words: "that your hearing should testify against you or your sight or your skins." He said: "You will be called on the Day of Resurrection with your mouths sealed with a seal (fidam). The first thing that will speak about a person is his thigh and his palm." Abd Allah ibn Abd al-A'la [[As it is in the originals, and in the book Adab al-Dunya wa al-Din: Abd al-A'la ibn Abd Allah al-Shami.]] al-Shami said: "He spoke well."

Life decreases while sins increase,
and the stumbles of a youth are reckoned, so he returns.

Can a man deny one sin
when his limbs are witnesses against him?

A person is asked about his years, so he desires
their reduction, and from death he flees.

From Ma'qil ibn Yasar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "There is no day that comes upon the son of Adam but it is called out: 'O son of Adam, I am a new creation, and I am a witness over you concerning what you do tomorrow. So do good in me, and I will bear witness for you tomorrow, for if I pass, you will never see me again.' And the night says the same." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz related it, and we have mentioned it in our book al-Tadhkira in the chapter on the testimony of the earth, the nights, the days, and the wealth.

Muhammad ibn Bashir said, and spoke well:

Your yesterday has passed as a just witness,
and this your day is a witness by your deeds.

If yesterday you committed an evil,
then follow it with good, and you will be praised.

Do not postpone doing good from you to tomorrow,
for perhaps tomorrow will come while you are gone.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that is your opinion which you held about your Lord; it has ruined you﴾, that is, it destroyed you and brought you down into the Fire. Qatada said: "Here 'al-zann' (opinion) means 'al-'ilm' (knowledge)." The Prophet ﷺ said: "None of you should die except while thinking well of Allah, for a people thought ill of their Lord and He destroyed them." That is the meaning of His words: "And that is your opinion which you held about your Lord; it has ruined you."

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "A people were diverted by wishful thinking until they left the world without any good deed, and one of them says: 'I think well of my Lord,' and he lies. If he had thought well, he would have done good deeds," and he recited the words of Allah the Exalted: "And that is your opinion which you held about your Lord; it has ruined you, so you became among the losers."

Qatada said: "Whoever among you can die while thinking well of his Lord, let him do so, for opinion is of two kinds: an opinion that saves and an opinion that ruins."

Umar ibn al-Khattab said regarding this verse: "These are people who persisted in disobedience and did not repent from it, and spoke of forgiveness, until they left the world bankrupt." Then he recited: "And that is your opinion which you held about your Lord; it has ruined you, so you became among the losers."

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So if they endure, the Fire is their abode﴾, that is: if they endure in the world upon the deeds of the people of the Fire, then the Fire is their abode. Its parallel is: ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ [al-Baqara: 175], as has already been explained [[See vol. 2, p. 236, second edition.]]. What indicates the lamenting is His words: "And if they seek to be pleased," because "al-musta'tab" is one who laments, and "al-mu'tab" is one whose reproach is accepted. Al-Nabigha said:

If I am wronged, it is by a slave whom I wronged;
if you are one who reproaches, then one like you is reproached.

That is: one like you is one who accepts reconciliation and return when he is asked. Al-Khalil said: "al-'itab" is addressing one who feels he has a claim, and discussing a grievance. You say: "I reproached him, a reproach," and among them there is "u'tuba," with which they reproach one another. It is said: when they reproach one another, reproach sets right what is between them. "A'tabani fulan" means: he returned to my pleasure, turning back from the offense, and its noun is "al-'utba," which is the return of the one reproached to what pleases the one who reproaches. "Istatab" and "a'tab" have the same meaning, and "istatab" also means he sought to be pleased. You say: "I sought his pleasure, so he pleased me," that is, "I sought his satisfaction, so he satisfied me." So the meaning of "and if they seek to be pleased" is: if they seek satisfaction, that will not benefit them, but they must have the Fire. In the tafsir works: "And if they ask their Lord to withdraw (yastaqiluu), then they are not among those who are granted withdrawal." Ubayd ibn Umayr and Abu al-Aliya recited "wa in yustatabu" with an open second ta' and a damma on the ya' as the passive verb, "fa ma hum min al-mu'tabin" with a kasra on the ta': that is, if Allah grants them withdrawal and returns them to the world, they would not act in obedience to Him, because of the wretchedness that was decreed for them in Allah's knowledge. Tha'lab said: "It is said: 'a'tab' when he became angry, and 'a'tab' when he was pleased."

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We assigned to them companions﴾. Al-Naqqash said: that is, We prepared for them devils. It has been said: We set over them companions who make their sins appear attractive to them, and these companions are from the jinn and the devils, and from mankind also. That is, We caused them to have companions. It is said: "Qayyada Allah fulanan li-fulan" means Allah brought him to him and made him available to him, and from this is His words: ﴿And We assigned to them companions﴾. Al-Qushayri said: It is said: "Qayyada Allah li rizqan," meaning He made it available as I was seeking it. "Al-taqyid" is substitution, and from it comes "al-muqayada" (exchange): "qayadtu al-rajul muqayadatan," meaning I exchanged goods with the man, and they are two "qayd," as you say two "bay'" (sales).

﴿And they made attractive to them what was before them﴾ of the affairs of the world, so they made it fair-seeming to them until they preferred it over the Hereafter. ﴿And what was behind them﴾: they made attractive to them what would come after their death, and called them to deny the matters of the Hereafter, from Mujahid. It has been said: the meaning is: ﴿We assigned to them companions﴾ in the Fire, ﴿and they made attractive to them﴾ their deeds in the world. The meaning is: We decreed that this would happen to them and judged it upon them. It has been said: the meaning is: We made them need companions, that is, We made the poor need the rich so that he might obtain from him, and the rich need the poor so that he might be helped by him, so some of them made the disobediences attractive to others. Ibn Abbas said: "What was before them" is their denial of the matters of the Hereafter, "and what was behind them" is procrastination and encouragement toward the world. Al-Zajjaj said: "What was before them" is what they had done, "and what was behind them" is what they had resolved to do. The saying of Mujahid has already been mentioned. It has been said: the meaning is that they had like the disobediences that preceded, "and what was behind them" is what would be done after them.

﴿And the word has come true against them, among nations﴾, that is: there became due upon them of the punishment what became due upon the nations before them who disbelieved, like their disbelief. It has been said: "fi" here means "ma'a" (with), so the meaning is: they are included with the disbelieving nations before them in what they entered into. It has been said: "fi umam" means "in a multitude of nations," and similar is the saying of the poet [[He is Amr ibn Udhayna.]]:

If you are one who has failed in the best of conduct,
then you are among others who have been turned away.

He means: you are among a multitude of others, and you are not unique in that. The place of "fi umam" is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "alayhim," that is: the word has come true against them, being among a multitude of nations. ﴿Indeed they were losers﴾: in their deeds in the world, and in their souls and their families on the Day of Resurrection.

Life decreases while sins increase,

when his limbs are witnesses against him?

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verses 26–29:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Quran, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may overcome."﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, informed of the disbelief of the people of Hud, Salih and others, He informed of the polytheists of Quraysh, that they denied the Quran and said: "Do not listen." It was also said that the meaning of "do not listen" is "do not obey," as one says: "I listened to you," meaning "I obeyed you." As for "and make noise during it," Ibn Abbas said: Abu Jahl said, "When Muhammad recites, shout at him so that he does not know what he is saying." It was also said: they did this when the Quran overwhelmed them. Mujahid said: the meaning of "and make noise during it" is by whistling, clapping, and confusing speech, until it becomes mere noise. Al-Dahhak said: Speak much, so that what he says becomes confused for him. Abu al-Aliyah and Ibn Abbas also said: Find fault with it and disparage it. "Perhaps you may overcome" Muhammad in his recitation, so that he will not prevail and will not win hearts. Isa ibn Umar, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah and Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi read "wa-l-ghaw" with a damma on the ghayn, and it is a dialect of laghā yalghū. The reading of the majority is from laghiya yalghā. Al-Harawi said: His saying "wa-l-ghaw fihi" — it was said: oppose him with speech that is not understood. One says: laghawtu, alghū and alghā, laghiya yalghā, three dialects. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 41, verses 30–32:**

His saying, may He be exalted: "Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remain steadfast..." ʿAtaʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. The reason was that the polytheists said, "Our Lord is Allah, and the angels are His daughters, and these are our intercessors with Allah," and they did not remain steadfast. Abu Bakr said, "Our Lord is Allah alone, without partner, and Muhammad (ﷺ) is His servant and Messenger," and he remained steadfast.

In al-Tirmidhi, it is reported from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited, "Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remain steadfast," and said: "People have said it, then most of them disbelieved. Whoever dies upon it is among those who remained steadfast."(2) He said: this is a gharib (strange) hadith.

It is also related concerning this verse, from the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman and ʿAli, the meaning of "remained steadfast." In Sahih Muslim, it is reported from Sufyan ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Thaqafi who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying in Islam about which I will not ask anyone after you,'" and in another narration, "other than you." He said: "Say, 'I have believed in Allah,' then be steadfast." Al-Tirmidhi added: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what is the thing you fear most for me?" So he took hold of his own tongue and said, "This."

It is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said concerning "then remained steadfast": they did not associate anything with Allah. Al-Aswad ibn Hilal reported from him that he said to his companions: "What do you say about these two verses: 'Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast,' and 'Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing'?" They said: "They remained steadfast, so they did not sin, and they did not mix their belief with error." Abu Bakr said: "You have taken them to a meaning other than their intended meaning. 'Who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast' means they did not turn to any god other than Him. 'And did not mix their belief' means with shirk. 'Those will have security, and they are guided.'"

It is related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said from the pulpit while delivering a sermon: "Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' then remain steadfast," and he said: "They remained steadfast, by Allah, upon the path toward obedience to Him, then they did not swerve like foxes swerve."

ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Then they made their deeds sincerely for Allah." ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Then they performed the obligations."

The sayings of the Tabiʿun (the Successors) are similar in meaning. Ibn Zayd and Qatadah said: they remained steadfast in obedience to Allah. Al-Hasan said: they remained steadfast on the command of Allah, so they acted in obedience to Him and avoided His disobedience. Mujahid and ʿIkrimah said: they remained steadfast upon the testimony that there is no god but Allah, until they died. Sufyan al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they said. Al-Rabiʿ said: they turned away from everything other than Allah. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: they renounced the transient and desired the everlasting. It was also said: they remained steadfast secretly as they remained steadfast openly. It was also said: they remained steadfast in action as they remained steadfast in speech.

Anas said: when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They are my Ummah, and by the Lord of the Kaʿbah." Imam Ibn Fawrak said: the sin in "istaqamu" is the sin of seeking, like in "istasqa" (he asked for water), meaning they asked Allah to keep them firm upon the religion. Al-Hasan, whenever he recited this verse, would say: "O Allah, You are our Lord, so grant us steadfastness."

I say: although these sayings overlap, their summary is: be upright in obedience to Allah in belief, speech and action, and persist in that.

His saying, "The angels will descend upon them." Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: at the time of death. Muqatil and Qatadah said: when they rise from their graves for the Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is glad tidings they will receive from the angels in the Hereafter. Waki and Ibn Zayd said: the glad tidings are in three situations: at death, in the grave, and at the Resurrection.

"Do not fear," meaning, with the preposition: "that do not fear," so the preposition is omitted. Mujahid said: do not fear death.

"And do not grieve," over your children, for Allah is your successor over them. ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah said: do not fear the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted. ʿIkrimah said: do not fear your imam (leader), and do not grieve over your sins.

"And rejoice in the Paradise which you were promised."

His saying, may He be exalted: "We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter." That is, the angels who descend upon them with glad tidings say to them, "We are your allies."

Mujahid said: that is, we are your companions who were with you in this world; when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will say, "We will not leave you until we bring you into Paradise." Al-Suddi said: that is, we are the guardians of your deeds in this world, and your allies in the Hereafter. It is also possible that this is from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, for Allah is the Protector and Master of the believers.

"And for you therein is whatever your souls desire," that is, of delights. "And for you therein is whatever you request," meaning you ask for and wish for. "As a welcome," that is, provision and hospitality. This has already been discussed in Surah Al ʿImran.(1) It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning "We have sent it down as a welcome." It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It was also said: it is the plural of nazil (one who descends), meaning, "For you is what you request, descending," so it is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "tadduʿun" or of the genitive pronoun in "lakum" (for you).

(1) [See vol. 4, p. 321, first or second edition.]

It is also related concerning this verse, from the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman and ʿAli, the meaning of "remained steadfast." In Sahih Muslim, it is reported from Sufyan ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Thaqafi who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying in Islam about which I will not ask anyone after you,'" and in another narration, "other than you." He said: "Say, 'I have believed in Allah,' then be steadfast." Al-Tirmidhi added: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what is the thing you fear most for me?" So he took hold of his own tongue and said, "This."

It is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said concerning "then remained steadfast": they did not associate anything with Allah. Al-Aswad ibn Hilal reported from him that he said to his companions: "What do you say about these two verses: 'Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast,' and 'Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing'?" They said: "They remained steadfast, so they did not sin, and they did not mix their belief with error." Abu Bakr said: "You have taken them to a meaning other than their intended meaning. 'Who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast' means they did not turn to any god other than Him. 'And did not mix their belief' means with shirk. 'Those will have security, and they are guided.'"

It is related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said from the pulpit while delivering a sermon: "Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' then remain steadfast," and he said: "They remained steadfast, by Allah, upon the path toward obedience to Him, then they did not swerve like foxes swerve."

ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Then they made their deeds sincerely for Allah." ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Then they performed the obligations."

The sayings of the Tabiʿun (the Successors) are similar in meaning. Ibn Zayd and Qatadah said: they remained steadfast in obedience to Allah. Al-Hasan said: they remained steadfast on the command of Allah, so they acted in obedience to Him and avoided His disobedience. Mujahid and ʿIkrimah said: they remained steadfast upon the testimony that there is no god but Allah, until they died. Sufyan al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they said. Al-Rabiʿ said: they turned away from everything other than Allah. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: they renounced the transient and desired the everlasting. It was also said: they remained steadfast secretly as they remained steadfast openly. It was also said: they remained steadfast in action as they remained steadfast in speech.

Anas said: when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They are my Ummah, and by the Lord of the Kaʿbah." Imam Ibn Fawrak said: the sin in "istaqamu" is the sin of seeking, like in "istasqa" (he asked for water), meaning they asked Allah to keep them firm upon the religion. Al-Hasan, whenever he recited this verse, would say: "O Allah, You are our Lord, so grant us steadfastness."

I say: although these sayings overlap, their summary is: be upright in obedience to Allah in belief, speech and action, and persist in that.

His saying, "The angels will descend upon them." Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: at the time of death. Muqatil and Qatadah said: when they rise from their graves for the Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is glad tidings they will receive from the angels in the Hereafter. Waki and Ibn Zayd said: the glad tidings are in three situations: at death, in the grave, and at the Resurrection.

"Do not fear," meaning, with the preposition: "that do not fear," so the preposition is omitted. Mujahid said: do not fear death.

"And do not grieve," over your children, for Allah is your successor over them. ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah said: do not fear the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted. ʿIkrimah said: do not fear your imam (leader), and do not grieve over your sins.

"And rejoice in the Paradise which you were promised."

His saying, may He be exalted: "We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter." That is, the angels who descend upon them with glad tidings say to them, "We are your allies."

Mujahid said: that is, we are your companions who were with you in this world; when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will say, "We will not leave you until we bring you into Paradise." Al-Suddi said: that is, we are the guardians of your deeds in this world, and your allies in the Hereafter. It is also possible that this is from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, for Allah is the Protector and Master of the believers.

"And for you therein is whatever your souls desire," that is, of delights. "And for you therein is whatever you request," meaning you ask for and wish for. "As a welcome," that is, provision and hospitality. This has already been discussed in Surah Al ʿImran.(1) It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning "We have sent it down as a welcome." It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It was also said: it is the plural of nazil (one who descends), meaning, "For you is what you request, descending," so it is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "tadduʿun" or of the genitive pronoun in "lakum" (for you).

(1) [See vol. 4, p. 321, first or second edition.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 33–36:

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah and does righteous work and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ This is a rebuke to those who advised one another to engage in idle talk concerning the Qur'an. The meaning is: what speech is better than the Qur'an, and who is better in speech than the caller to Allah and to His obedience, who is Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Sirin, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan said: it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When al-Hasan recited this verse he would say: "This is the Messenger of Allah, this is the beloved of Allah, this is the friend of Allah, this is the chosen one of Allah, this is the best choice of Allah. By Allah, he is the most beloved of the people of the earth to Allah. He responded to Allah in His call, and he called the people to what he responded to."

'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), 'Ikrimah, Qays ibn Abi Hazim and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (those who call the adhan). Fudayl ibn Rufayda said: "I was a muezzin for the companions of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and 'Asim ibn Hubayra said to me: When you give the adhan and say, 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah,' then say, 'and I am of the Muslims,'" and then he recited this verse.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The first view is more sound, because the verse is Meccan and the adhan is Medinan. It includes them only in meaning, not that it was the intended reference at the time of the utterance. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq also enters within it when he said concerning the Prophet ﷺ, while the accursed one was choking him: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. And it encompasses every good speech in which the mention of tawhid and faith is found.

I say: there is a third view, and it is the best of them. Al-Hasan said: this verse is general concerning everyone who calls to Allah. Likewise Qays ibn Abi Hazim said: it was revealed concerning every believer.

He said: the meaning of "and does righteous work" is prayer between the adhan and the iqamah. Abu Umamah also said this, saying: "He prayed two rak'ahs between the adhan and the iqamah." 'Ikrimah said: "and does righteous work" means he prayed and fasted. Al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties.

I say: this is the best of them, together with avoiding the prohibitions and abundance of the recommended acts. And Allah knows best.

﴿And who says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾. Ibn al-'Arabi said: What precedes indicates Islam, but since calling (du'a') may be by speech and by the sword, and may be for belief or for proof, and since action may be for show or for sincerity, this shows that it is necessary to explicitly declare belief in Allah in all of that, and that the action is for His sake.

Issue: When the Exalted said, ﴿"Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ and did not say to him, "Make a condition: if Allah wills," this constitutes a refutation of those who say, "I am a Muslim, if Allah wills."

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Good and evil are not equal.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "la" is superfluous, meaning "and good and evil are not equal." He cited:

"The Messenger of Allah was not pleased with their deed, nor were the two good ones, Abu Bakr and 'Umar."

He meant Abu Bakr and 'Umar. That is, what you are upon of tawhid is not equal to what the polytheists are upon of shirk. Ibn 'Abbas said: the good (ḥasanah) is "There is no god but Allah," and the evil (sayyi'ah) is shirk. It was also said: the good is obedience and the evil is shirk, and this is the same as the first. It was said: the good is forbearance and the evil is harshness. It was said: the good is pardon and the evil is retaliation. Al-Dahhak said: the good is knowledge and the evil is obscenity. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the good is love of the family of the Messenger, and the evil is hatred of them.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Repel with that which is better﴾ was abrogated by the verse of the sword, and what remains recommended from it is good companionship, tolerance and overlooking. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, repel with your forbearance the ignorance of one who acts ignorantly toward you. He also said: it is a man who insults another, and the other says, "If you are truthful, may Allah forgive me; and if you are lying, may Allah forgive you." Likewise it is related in a report that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said this to a man who had insulted him. Mujahid said: "with that which is better" means greeting one who is hostile to you when you meet him, and 'Ata' said the same. A third view, mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi in al-Ahkam, is handshaking. And there is a report: "Shake hands, and rancour will depart." Malik did not approve of handshaking. He met Sufyan and they discussed it, and Sufyan said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ shook hands with Ja'far when he came from the land of Abyssinia. Malik said to him: That was specific. Sufyan said to him: What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made specific does not restrict us, and what he made general does not generalise for us; handshaking is established, so there is no basis for denying it. Qatadah narrated: I said to Anas, "Was there handshaking among the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said: "Yes." This is a sound hadith. And there is a report: "Among the perfection of love is taking the hand." And from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who is a leading imam, from al-Zuhri from 'Urwah from 'Aishah, she said: Zayd ibn Harithah came to Medina while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in my house, and he knocked on the door, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ got up to him naked, dragging his garment—by Allah, I never saw him naked before or after that—and he embraced him and kissed him.

I say: it has been related from Malik the permissibility of handshaking, and a group of scholars act upon it. This has passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 266, first or second edition.]], and we mentioned there the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No two Muslims meet and one of them takes the hand of his companion out of affection and sincere advice between them, except that their sins fall away between them."

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Then, the one between you and him is enmity, as if he were a close friend.﴾ That is, a near, intimate friend. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who used to harm the Prophet ﷺ; he became a friend to him after being an enemy, through the affinity (musahara) that occurred between him and the Prophet ﷺ, and then he embraced Islam and became a close friend in Islam through kinship. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who used to harm the Prophet ﷺ, so Allah commanded him to be patient with him and to pardon him; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The first view was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri, and it is more apparent, due to His statement: ﴿Then, the one between you and him is enmity, as if he were a close friend.﴾ It was also said: this was before the command to fight. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah commanded him in this verse to be patient at anger, forbearing at ignorance, and forgiving at offence; when people do that, Allah protects them from Satan, and their enemy submits to them. It is related that a man insulted Qanbar, the freedman of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and 'Ali called out: "O Qanbar, leave your insulter, and turn away from him; you will please the Merciful and anger Satan, and you will punish your insulter, for the fool is not punished with anything like silence toward him." They recited:

"And to refrain from insulting the base, out of nobility, is more harmful to him than insulting him when he is insulted."

Another said:

"Nothing is dearer to a fool, when he reviles the noble, than a reply, Leaving the fool without an answer is more painful to the fool than reviling."

Mahmud al-Warraq said:

"I shall compel myself to pardon every wrongdoer, though his offences be many before me. People are none but one of three: a noble, one who is ennobled, and an equal who contends. As for the one above me, I recognise his rank, and I follow in regard to him the truth, and the truth is binding. As for the one below me, if he speaks, I preserve my honour from answering him, though a blamer blame. As for my equal, if he slips or errs, I show favour, for favour is judged by forbearance."

﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient﴾, meaning this noble deed and this excellent trait, by restraining anger and bearing harm. ﴿And none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾, that is, a great share of good; Ibn 'Abbas said this. Qatadah and Mujahid said: "the great fortune" is Paradise. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, no fortune has ever been greater than Paradise. It was also said that the pronoun in "is granted it" refers to Paradise, meaning none is granted it except the patient; the meaning is close.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you﴾ has been fully discussed earlier at the end of "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 347 onward, first or second edition.]]. ﴿Then seek refuge in Allah﴾ from his plot and evil. ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing﴾ of your seeking refuge, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of your deeds and your words.

He also said: it is a man who insults another, and the other says, "If you are truthful, may Allah forgive me; and if you are lying, may Allah forgive you." Likewise it is related in a report that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said this to a man who had insulted him. Mujahid said: "with that which is better" means greeting one who is hostile to you when you meet him, and 'Ata' said the same. A third view, mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi in al-Ahkam, is handshaking. And there is a report: "Shake hands, and rancour will depart." Malik did not approve of handshaking. He met Sufyan and they discussed it, and Sufyan said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ shook hands with Ja'far when he came from the land of Abyssinia. Malik said to him: That was specific. Sufyan said to him: What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made specific does not restrict us, and what he made general does not generalise for us; handshaking is established, so there is no basis for denying it. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who used to harm the Prophet ﷺ, so Allah commanded him to be patient with him and to pardon him; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Another said:

Mahmud al-Warraq said:

When al-Hasan recited this verse he would say: "This is the Messenger of Allah, this is the beloved of Allah, this is the friend of Allah, this is the chosen one of Allah, this is the best choice of Allah. 'Ikrimah said: "and does righteous work" means he prayed and fasted. Al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties.

I say: this is the best of them, together with avoiding the prohibitions and abundance of the recommended acts. And Allah knows best.
