Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 37–39:

Allah's words "And among His signs" (ayatihi): its indications (ʿalamatuhu), which point to His oneness and His power, "the night and the day, the sun and the moon." This has passed in more than one place [[See vol. 2, p. 192 and what follows, second edition.]]. Then He forbade prostrating to them, because although they are created, that is not due to any excellence in themselves that would make them deserving of worship alongside Allah, since their Creator is Allah. Had He willed, He would have annihilated them or obliterated their light. "And prostrate to Allah who created them" and fashioned them and subjected them to His service. The pronoun (al-kinaya) refers to the sun, the moon, the night and the day. It has been said that it refers to the sun and the moon specifically, because the two together are a plural. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the meaning of "the signs": "if it is Him you worship." It was feminine on the basis of the plural of multiplicity (jam' al-taktir), and it did not follow the method of giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine, because it refers to what is not rational. "But if they are arrogant," meaning the disbelievers, regarding prostration to Allah, "then those who are with your Lord," from among the angels, "glorify Him night and day, and they never tire" (la yas'amun), meaning they do not grow weary of His worship. Zuhayr said:

Called the burdens of life; and whoever lives
Eighty years, by your father, does not tire.

Issue: This verse is a verse of prostration without any disagreement, and they differed regarding the place of prostration in it. Malik said: its place is "if it is Him you worship," because it is connected to the command. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and others used to prostrate at the words "you worship." Ibn Wahb and al-Shafi'i said: its place is "and they never tire," because it is the completion of the statement and the ultimate point of worship and obedience. Abu Hanifa also said this. Ibn ʿAbbas used to prostrate at the words "they never tire." Ibn ʿUmar said: prostrate at the last of the two. Similarly it is narrated from Masruq, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, Abu Salih, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha and Zubayd al-Yamiyyayn [[This nisba is to Yama, a clan of Hamdan.]], al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin. Abu Wa'il, Qatada and Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah used to prostrate at the words "they never tire." Ibn al-ʿArabi said: the matter is close.

Issue: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned that this verse includes the prayer of the eclipse of the moon and the sun, because the Arabs used to say that the sun and the moon do not eclipse except for the death of a great person, so the Prophet ﷺ prayed the eclipse prayer. I say: the eclipse prayer is established in the Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim and others. They differed greatly regarding its manner because of the variation in the reports, and what is in Sahih Muslim on this suffices you, and it is the principal reference in the chapter. And Allah is the granter of success in what is right.

Allah's words: {And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled} The address is to every person of understanding, meaning: "and among His signs" that indicate He gives life to the dead, "that you see the earth humbled," i.e., dry and barren. This is the description of the earth with humility (khushu'). Al-Nabigha said:

Ashes like the kohl of the eye, which I could not make out except after much trouble, a hollow around a tent, its base broken down, humbled [[He likens the ashes to kohl because they blacken when their traces age and rain strikes them. The nawy is a trench around the tent. The jidhm is the base. Athlam means ruined. Khashi' means its traces have collapsed and become level with the ground. He means that the ashes had changed and he could only recognize them after lei, i.e., after effort and hardship.]]

The humbled earth is the dusty land that produces plants. A humbled town is one covered in dust with no dwelling in it. A humbled place. {And when We send down water upon it, it stirs} i.e., with vegetation, said Mujahid. It is said: the person stirred (ihtazza), i.e., moved, and from it:

You see him like the blade of a sword quivering with generosity, when you find no hope in the evil man.

{And it swells} i.e., rises and grows high before it sprouts. Mujahid said: it rises up from the plants after its death. On this interpretation there is inversion in the statement, and its sense is: it swelled and stirred. Stirring and swelling may occur before the emergence from the earth, and may occur after the plants come out onto the surface of the earth. Its swelling is its rising. A raised place is called rabwa and rabiya. The plant moves to emerge, then increases in its body by growing in length and breadth. Abu Ja'far and Khalid read "wa rabaʾat," and its meaning is "it grew large," from al-rabiʾa. It has been said: "stirred" means it rejoiced at the rain, and "swelled" means it was puffed up with plants. When the earth splits open with plants it is described as laughing, so it is permissible to describe it as rejoicing too. It is also permissible to say that swelling and stirring are one, and it is the state of the plants' emergence. This meaning has passed in "al-Hajj" [[See vol. 13, p. 13, first or second edition.]]. {Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead; indeed, He is over all things Competent} has been mentioned in more than one place [[See vol. 14, p. 45, first or second edition.]].

Allah's words: {And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled} The address is to every person of understanding, meaning: "and among His signs" that indicate He gives life to the dead, "that you see the earth humbled," i.e., dry and barren. This is the description of the earth with humility (khushu'). Al-Nabigha said:

Ashes like the kohl of the eye, which I could not make out except after much trouble, a hollow around a tent, its base broken down, humbled [[He likens the ashes to kohl because they blacken when their traces age and rain strikes them. The nawy is a trench around the tent. The jidhm is the base. Athlam means ruined. Khashi' means its traces have collapsed and become level with the ground. He means that the ashes had changed and he could only recognize them after lei, i.e., after effort and hardship.]]

The humbled earth is the dusty land that produces plants. A humbled town is one covered in dust with no dwelling in it. A humbled place. {And when We send down water upon it, it stirs} i.e., with vegetation, said Mujahid. It is said: the person stirred (ihtazza), i.e., moved, and from it:

You see him like the blade of a sword quivering with generosity, when you find no hope in the evil man.

{And it swells} i.e., rises and grows high before it sprouts. Mujahid said: it rises up from the plants after its death. On this interpretation there is inversion in the statement, and its sense is: it swelled and stirred. Stirring and swelling may occur before the emergence from the earth, and may occur after the plants come out onto the surface of the earth. Its swelling is its rising. A raised place is called rabwa and rabiya. The plant moves to emerge, then increases in its body by growing in length and breadth. Abu Ja'far and Khalid read "wa rabaʾat," and its meaning is "it grew large," from al-rabiʾa. It has been said: "stirred" means it rejoiced at the rain, and "swelled" means it was puffed up with plants. When the earth splits open with plants it is described as laughing, so it is permissible to describe it as rejoicing too. It is also permissible to say that swelling and stirring are one, and it is the state of the plants' emergence. This meaning has passed in "al-Hajj" [[See vol. 13, p. 13, first or second edition.]]. {Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead; indeed, He is over all things Competent} has been mentioned in more than one place [[See vol. 14, p. 45, first or second edition.]].

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 41, verses 40–43:**

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate from Our signs﴾. That is, they incline away from the truth regarding Our proofs. *Al-ilhad* (deviation) means inclining and turning away. From it comes *al-lahd* in the grave, because the side of the grave is inclined. It is said: *alhada fi din Allah*, meaning he deviated from it and turned away. *Lahada* is also a dialectal form of the same word. This refers to those who said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it" (cf. 41:26). They are the ones who deviated regarding its verses and inclined away from the truth. They said: "The Qur'an is not from Allah," or "It is poetry" or "It is sorcery." The verses are the verses of the Qur'an.

Mujahid said: "Those who deviate regarding Our signs" means, during the recitation of the Qur'an, with whistling, clapping, idle talk and singing.

Ibn Abbas said: it is the altering of speech and placing it in other than its proper place.

Qatadah said: "Those who deviate regarding Our signs" means those who lie regarding Our signs.

Al-Suddi said: they oppose and contend.

Ibn Zayd said: they associate partners with Allah and lie. The meanings are close to one another.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

It has also been said that "the signs" are the miracles, and this returns to the first meaning, since the Qur'an is a miracle.

﴿Is one who is thrown into the Fire on his face﴾: this is Abu Jahl according to Ibn Abbas and others.

﴿Or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ It has been said that this is the Prophet (ﷺ), as Muqatil said. It has been said that it is Ammar ibn Yasir. It has been said that it is Hamzah. It has been said that it is Umar ibn al-Khattab. It has been said that it is Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi. It has been said that it is the believers. It has been said that the verse is general: the one thrown into the Fire is the disbeliever, and the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection is the believer. This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

﴿Do whatever you will﴾: this is an imperative of threat, meaning: since you have come to know that the two are not equal, there must be a recompense for you.

﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾: a warning accompanied by a threat and a promise of punishment.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it has come to them﴾. The "Reminder" here is the Qur'an, according to all scholars, because it contains mention of what is needed of the rulings.

The predicate is omitted, and its estimated sense is [[an addition required by the context.]] "They are destroyed or punished." It has also been said that the predicate is ﴿They are called from a distant place﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. The statement "What is said to you" is interposed, then he returns to the Reminder and says: ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾ [41:44], then he says: ﴿They are called﴾ [41:44]. The first view is the preferred one. Al-Nahhas said: this is the view of all the grammarians, as far as I know.

﴿And indeed, it is a Mighty Book﴾: that is, mighty in the sight of Allah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and it is also reported from him: mighty from Allah. It has also been said: noble in the sight of Allah. It has been said: "Mighty" means that Allah has made it mighty, so falsehood cannot reach it. It has been said: it ought to be honoured and exalted, and nothing vain should be uttered in it. It has been said: "Mighty" means protected from Satan, so that he cannot alter it. This was said by al-Suddi. Muqatil said: it is protected from Satan and falsehood. Al-Suddi said: it is uncreated, so it has no like. Ibn Abbas also said: "Mighty" means that people are prevented from producing the like of it.

﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾: that is, no part of what Allah revealed before it can refute it, nor will anything be revealed after it that would nullify and abrogate it. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Al-Suddi and Qatadah said: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾ means Satan, ﴿from before it or behind it﴾: he cannot change it, nor add to it, nor subtract from it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: denial cannot approach it ﴿from before it or behind it﴾.

Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾ neither in what it reports of the past nor in what it reports of the future.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: ﴿from before it﴾ means from Allah, the Exalted, and ﴿nor from behind it﴾ means from Jibril (ﷺ) and from Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿A revelation from One who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "All-Wise" in His creation, "Praiseworthy" toward them. Qatadah said: "All-Wise" in His command, "Praiseworthy" toward His creation.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Nothing is said to you﴾, that is, of harm and denial, ﴿except what was said to the messengers before you﴾. He consoles His Prophet and comforts him. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is possessor of forgiveness﴾ for you and for your companions, ﴿and of painful punishment﴾, meaning for your enemies, a painful punishment.

It has also been said: that is, nothing is said to you about sincerity in worship to Allah except what was revealed to those before you. There is no disagreement among the revealed laws regarding what pertains to monotheism. This is like His saying: "And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should commit shirk, your work would surely be nullified" [39:65]. That is, you did not call them except to what all the prophets called to, so there is no sense in their denying it to you.

It has also been said: it is an interrogative, meaning: what is it that is said to you, ﴿except what was said to the messengers before you﴾?

It has also been said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾ is a new sentence, and what precedes it is a complete statement, when the predicate is implied.

It has also been said: it is connected to "what is said to you."

﴿Indeed, your Lord is possessor of forgiveness and of painful punishment﴾: that is, I was only commanded to warn and to give good news.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: "And if We had made it a Qur'an in a foreign tongue, they would have said, 'Why are its verses not made clear? What, a foreign tongue and an Arab?'" In this there are three issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We had made it a Qur'an in a foreign tongue﴾, meaning in the language of non-Arabs, ﴿they would have said, "Why are its verses not made clear?"﴾, meaning made clear in our language, for we are Arabs who do not understand the foreign tongue. So He made clear that He sent it down in their language so that the meaning of the inimitability (i'jaz) might be established through it, since they are the people most knowledgeable of the types of speech, in verse (nazm) and in prose (nathr). When they are unable to produce its equal, this is among the strongest proofs that it is from Allah. Had it been in the tongue of the non-Arabs, they would have said, "We have no knowledge of this tongue."

The second: Given that this is established, there is in it evidence that the Qur'an is Arabic, that it was revealed in the language of the Arabs, that it is not foreign, and that if it is translated from it into another language it is no longer the Qur'an.

The third: His saying, may He be exalted: "What, a foreign tongue and an Arab?" Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "a'jamiyyun wa 'arabiyy" with two light hamzas. The 'ajami is one who is not of the Arabs, whether eloquent or not eloquent, while the a'jami is one who does not speak clearly. Thus al-a'jam is the opposite of the eloquent (fasih), namely one who does not make his speech clear. It is said of a non-speaking animal that it is a'jam, and from this comes "the daytime prayer is 'ajma'," meaning that the recitation is not said aloud in it. So attribution to the a'jam was more emphatic, because the foreign man who is not of the Arabs may be eloquent in Arabic, and the Arab may be not eloquent, so attribution to the a'jami is more emphatic in clarity. The meaning is: "Is it a foreign Qur'an and an Arab prophet?" and it is a rhetorical question of denial.

Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Nasr ibn 'Asim, al-Mughirah and Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read "a'jamiyyun" with a single hamzah, as a statement. The meaning is: "Had its verses not been made clear," so that some of it would be Arabic which the Arabs understand and some foreign which the non-Arabs understand.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that he said: The Quraysh said, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down as foreign and Arabic, so that some of its verses would be foreign and some of its verses Arabic?" Then the verse was revealed. And some words from every language were sent down in the Qur'an. Among them is "sijjil," which is Persian, and its origin is sang-i gil, meaning clay and stone. Among them is "firdaws," which is Roman (Greek), and likewise "qistas."

The people of the Hijaz, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Dhakwan and Hafs read it as an interrogative, except that they softened the hamzah according to their principles. The correct reading is the interrogative reading. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing﴾. Allah informed that the Qur'an is guidance and healing for everyone who believes in it, from doubt, suspicion and ailments. "And as for those who do not believe, in their ears is a deafness" (waqr), meaning deafness to hearing the Qur'an. For this reason they agreed to talk noisily during it. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it increases the wrongdoers in nothing but loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82]. It has already been discussed fully [[See vol. 10, p. 315 ff., first or second edition.]]. The common reading is "'aman" as a verbal noun. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, 'Amr ibn al-'As, Mu'awiyah and Sulayman ibn Qattah read "wa huwa 'alayhim 'amin" with a kasrah on the mim, meaning that it is not clear to them. Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading, because of the consensus of people upon it, and because of His earlier saying "guidance and healing." Had it been "hadin wa shafin," the kasrah in "'ama" would be better, so that it would be a qualifier like them. Its sense: "And those who do not believe," in refusing to accept it, are like one who has deafness in his ears, "and it" (meaning the Qur'an) "is for them a blindness," because they do not understand. So the mudaf (the governed noun) is omitted. It was also said: the wiqr upon them is a blindness.

"Those are called from a far place." This is said of one who does not understand an illustration. The lexicographers relate that it is said to one who understands: "You hear from nearby," and to one who does not understand: "You are called from afar," meaning as if he is being called from a place far from him, so he neither hears the call nor understands it. Al-Dahhak said: "They are called" on the Day of Resurrection by their most hideous names, "from a far place," so that this is more intense for their rebuke and disgrace. It was also said: whoever does not reflect upon the Qur'an becomes like the blind and deaf, and he is called from a far place, so the caller's voice cuts off from him while he has not heard. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mujahid said: meaning far from their hearts. In the tafsir: it is as if they are called from the sky and they do not hear. Al-Naqqash related this meaning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 45–46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah, "but it was disputed about," that is, some people believed in it and some people denied it. The pronoun refers to the Book, and it is a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: do not let the disagreement of your people about your Book grieve you, for those before them also disagreed about their Book. It was also said that the pronoun refers to Musa. ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, that is, concerning their being granted respite, ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾, that is, by hastening the punishment. ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾, concerning the Qur'an, ﴿disquieting﴾, that is, of intense suspicion. This has already been discussed [see vol. 9, p. 59, first or second edition]. Al-Kalbi said regarding this verse: Were it not that Allah delayed the punishment of this community until the Day of Resurrection, the punishment would have come upon them as it did to other nations. It was also said: the delay of the punishment is because of the believers who will come forth from their loins. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self, and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾. This is a conditional sentence, and its response is "and whoever does evil, it is against it." Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, is free of need for the obedience of His servants; so whoever obeys, the reward is for him, and whoever does evil, the punishment is upon him. ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾. He negated injustice from Himself, may He be glorified and exalted, both little and much, and when the intensive form is negated, other forms are negated too. Its evidence is His saying, the Truth: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all﴾ [Yunus: 44]. The trustworthy narrators and the firm imams related, from the upright ascetic, from the trustworthy one of the earth, from the trustworthy one of the heaven, from the Lord, majestic is His majesty: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another," and the hadith continues. Moreover, He is the Wise, the Sovereign, and what the sovereign does in his dominion is not subject to objection, since He has the right to dispose of His dominion as He wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verses 47–48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning the time of its occurrence. This is because they said: "O Muhammad, if you are a prophet, tell us when the Hour will come." So it was revealed: "No fruit comes out of its sheaths." The "min" (from) here is zā'idah (superfluous, an extra particle), meaning: no fruit comes out. "From its sheaths" means from its coverings. So al-akmam (the sheaths) are the coverings of the fruit, singular kummah, and it is every container for property or other things. For this reason the membrane of the spathe, that is its outer covering from which the fruit splits open, is called a kummah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The kummah is the outer spathe before it splits; once it has split, it is no longer a kummah." More explanation of this will come in surah [al-Rahman [in the commentary on His saying: "And the palm tree with its sheaths" (verse 11)]].

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "min thamarat" in the plural. The rest read "thamarah" in the singular, but the intended meaning is the plural, because of His saying: "Nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge" (and the intended meaning is plural). He says: "To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour," just as the knowledge of the fruits and of births is referred to Him.

"And the Day He calls to them": that is, God calls to the polytheists, "Where are My partners?" those whom you claimed in the world to be gods that intercede. "They say": meaning the idols. It was also said that it means the polytheists. It is possible that He intends all of them, the worshipper and the worshipped. "We have informed You" means we have made You hear and made You know. It is said: adhana, yu'dhinu, meaning he informed, when he gave notice. The poet said:

[He is al-Harith ibn Hilzah, and the verse is the opening line of his mu'allaqah.]

"Asma' has announced to us her parting,
Many a dweller, of whom tiredness of staying is felt."

"None of us is a witness": that is, we inform You that none of us bears witness that You have a partner. When they witnessed the Resurrection, they disowned the idols, and the idols disowned them, as has been mentioned in more than one place [see vol. 13, pp. 303 ff., first or second edition]. "And what they used to invoke before has strayed from them" meaning: what they used to call upon in the world has vanished from them. "And they know" meaning: they are certain and aware "that there is for them no escape" meaning: no escape from the Fire. Here "ma" is a harf (particle) and not an ism (noun), so the verb of thinking (zanna) does not govern it, and the verb is treated as mulgha (nullified). The sense is: and they know that they have no escape and no refuge. It is said: haasa yahīsu, haysan and mahīsan, when he fled. It was also said that the zann (assumption) here is the kind that means the stronger opinion: they do not doubt that they are the people of the Fire, but they hope that they will come out of it. It is not unlikely that they have an assumption and hope until they are despaired.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 41, verse 49–51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾, meaning he does not grow weary of asking Him for good. Here "good" (al-khayr) refers to wealth, health, authority and honour. Al-Suddi said: "Man" (al-insan) here is intended to mean the disbeliever. It was also said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. And it was said: Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, and Umayya ibn Khalaf. In the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is read: "Man does not tire of asking for wealth" (al-mal). ﴿But when evil touches him﴾, namely poverty or sickness, ﴿he despairs﴾ of God's mercy (ya'us, from rawh Allah), ﴿and is hopeless﴾ (qanut) of His mercy. It was also said: "despairs" (ya'us) means despairing of the answering of supplication, and "hopeless" (qanut) means thinking ill of his Lord. It was also said: "despairs" means he has lost hope that the harm he suffers will be removed, and "hopeless" means he thinks it will last. The meanings are close.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us﴾, meaning ease, prosperity and wealth, ﴿after some hardship had touched him﴾, meaning harm, illness, distress and poverty, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, meaning: this is something I deserve from God because of His pleasure with my deeds. Thus he sees the blessing as something necessarily owed by God, the Exalted, and he does not know that He has tested him with blessing and affliction, so that his gratitude and patience might be made manifest. Ibn Abbas said: "This is mine" means "this is from me." ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have with Him the best (al-husna)﴾, meaning Paradise, and the lam is for emphasis. He wishes for wishes without works. Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib said: The disbeliever has two wishes. In this world he says: "Even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have with Him the best." And in the Hereafter he says: ﴿Would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord and we would be among the believers﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and "Would that I had been dust" [al-Naba': 40].

﴿So We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, meaning We will surely recompense them. It is an oath which God swore. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe torment﴾, meaning a harsh one.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, meaning the disbeliever, ﴿he turns away and withdraws to his side﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He means Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a and Umayya ibn Khalaf, who turned away from Islam and kept far from it. The meaning of "withdraws to his side" (na'a bi-janibihi) is that he holds himself aloof from submitting to the truth and is arrogant towards the prophets of God. It was said: "na'a" means he kept far away. It is said: nd'a and na'aytu 'anhu nay'an, meaning I kept far from him; and an'aytuhu, fa-intana, I made him distant so he became far; and tana'aw, they kept far from one another; and al-muntana' is the distant place. Al-Nabigha said:

"Indeed you are like the night which overtakes me, / if I think that the distance from you is wide."

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read "nā'a bi-janibihi" with an alif before the hamza. It may be from "nā'a", meaning to rise up, and it may be by transposing the hamza, with the same meaning as the first. ﴿And when evil touches him﴾, meaning harm befalls him, ﴿then he is one of abundant (ʿarid) supplication﴾, meaning much. The Arabs use length and breadth to mean abundance; it is said: so-and-so lengthened his speech and widened (a'rada) in supplication when he did much. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿Then he is one of abundant (ʿarid) supplication﴾ means one of humble entreaty and calling for help. The disbeliever knows his Lord in affliction, and does not know Him in ease.

His words, Exalted is He: "We will show them Our signs on the horizons" meaning the signs of Our oneness and Our power, "on the horizons" meaning the ruined dwellings of the earlier nations, "and within themselves" meaning through afflictions and diseases.

Ibn Zayd said: "on the horizons" refers to the signs of the sky, "and within themselves" refers to the events of the earth.

Mujahid said: "on the horizons" refers to the conquest of the towns. God, Mighty and Majestic, facilitated for His Messenger ﷺ, and for the caliphs after him and the helpers of his religion, the conquests across the horizons of the world and the lands of the East and West in general, and in the region of the West in particular, of a kind that was not made easy for any of the earth's caliphs before them; and [the victory] over tyrants and Persian kings, and the triumph of their few over their many, and the empowering of their weak over their strong, and the carrying out through their hands of matters outside the customary and beyond ordinary habits. "And within themselves" refers to the conquest of Mecca. This is the choice of al-Tabari.

Al-Minhal ibn Amr and al-Suddi also said this.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "on the horizons" refers to the battles of God among the nations, "and within themselves" refers to the day of Badr.

Ata and Ibn Zayd also said: "on the horizons" means the regions of the heavens and the earth, from the sun, the moon, the stars, night and day, the winds, the rains, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, plants, trees, mountains, seas and others.

A man is called afaqi (with an open hamza and fa) if he is from the horizons of the earth. This was related by Abu Nasr. Some say ufuqi with a damma, and this is the analogical form. Someone other than al-Jawhari recited:

"We have taken the horizons of the sky over you,
for us are its two moons and the rising stars."

"And within themselves": from the subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom, even in the passage of the excrement and urine. For a man drinks and eats from one place, and that is distinguished into two places. Also [there is] the wondrous craftsmanship and wisdom of God in his two eyes, which are a drop of water, by which he looks from the sky to the earth at a distance of five hundred years, and in his two ears, by which he distinguishes between different sounds, and other wondrous wisdom of God in him.

It has also been said: "and within themselves" refers to their being drops of semen, and to the other transformations of their states, as was explained earlier in [al-Mu'minun] [[See vol. 12, p. 109, first or second edition.]].

[First] that it is the Qur'an.
[Second] Islam, which the Messenger brought them and to which he called them.
[Third] that what God shows them and what He does of that is the truth.
[Fourth] that Muhammad ﷺ is the true Messenger.

﴿Is it not sufficient that your Lord is witness over all things?﴾ In the position of the nominative case, as the subject of "yakfi" (suffice). And "annahu" (that He) is an apposition to "rabbika" (your Lord). It is in the nominative if you consider it an apposition to the position [of the subject], and in the genitive if you consider it an apposition to the wording. It may also be in the accusative, with the preposition "li" omitted. The meaning: "Has not your Lord sufficed them, by what He has shown them of His oneness, because He is 'witness over all things'? It has been said: the meaning is "Has not your Lord sufficed," O Muhammad, that He is a witness over the deeds of the disbelievers. It has also been said: "Has not your Lord sufficed" as a witness that the Qur'an is from God. It has also been said: "Has not your Lord sufficed that He is over all things" of what the servant does, "a witness"? The word "shahid" (witness) means "knowing," or it derives from "shahada" (testimony), which is presence.

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾ that is, in the Hereafter. Al-Suddi said: that is, about the Resurrection.

﴿Unquestionably, He encompasses all things﴾ that is, His knowledge has encompassed all things. Al-Suddi said this. Al-Kalbi said: His power has encompassed all things.

Al-Khattabi said: He is the One whose power has encompassed all His creation, and who has encompassed all things in knowledge, and has counted all things in number. This name occurs most often in the context of threat. Its reality is encompassing all things and uprooting what is encompassed. Its root is muhit, the vowel of the ya' was moved to the ha' and it was made quiescent. It is said from it: ahata, yuhitu, ihatatan and haytatan. From this comes ha'it al-dar (the wall of the house), which its people surround. And "the horses encircled so-and-so" when they take a position besieging him from every direction. From this is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf 18:42]. And God knows best the correct meaning of that.
